title: Woolworths charged over NT crash between forklift, motorcyclist
description: Woolworths has been hit with a string of workplace safety charges after one of the supermarket giant's forklift operators allegedly struck a motorcyclist on a public road, causing "serious injuries", in 2025.

author: James Elton
full_text: Woolworths is facing a string of work health and safety charges as Northern Territory WorkSafe alleges one of its employees struck a motorcycle with a forklift on a public road in Katherine last year. A spokesperson for the workplace safety regulator says the motorcyclist was taken to hospital with "serious injuries" and alleges the supermarket giant breached its duty of care. What's next? The case will return to court in September. If the prosecution is successful, Woolworths could be liable for a penalty of up to $4.5 million. Northern Territory WorkSafe has charged Woolworths with a series of negligence offences after a forklift driver allegedly crashed into a motorcycle on a public road in the centre of Katherine, just outside the supermarket's loading dock. A spokesperson for the NT workplace safety regulator said in a statement the motorcyclist was taken to hospital and suffered "serious injuries" as a result of the crash in the town, located 300 kilometres south of Darwin, in July last year. The spokesperson said the Woolworths employee had attempted to drive the forklift "across a public road" behind the shop as a delivery truck was entering the loading dock. Images captured by the ABC at the time show a red motorcycle on its side in the centre of the street, with a forklift parked nearby. Paramedics were later seen putting the rider into the back of an ambulance on a stretcher. Woolworths is facing a total of four charges, including failing in a primary duty of care and failing in a duty involving management or control of a workplace, which combined carry a maximum penalty of $4.5 million. Under the NT Work Health and Safety Act, businesses have a duty to make sure "other persons", beyond their own workers, are not unreasonably put at risk through their operations. The Act also requires companies to ensure the "safe use, handling and storage" of machinery. Where a WorkSafe prosecution is successful, fines are usually paid into general government revenue; but some of the money can also go towards compensation for the injured person, as happened in a 2021 case brought against an NT cattle mustering contractor. The Woolworths charges were mentioned in the Katherine Local Court today before the case was adjourned until September 23. In a statement, a spokesperson for the supermarket giant said it took "our responsibility for workplace safety very seriously".
